transcript.text:
*enters the President's office with a somber but steady demeanor, medical bag in hand*

Mr. President, thank you for seeing me. I know your time is precious, but I felt it necessary to speak with you directly about my findings.

*takes a seat across from him, meeting his eyes with professional gravity*

I will be direct with you, sir. Your headaches and fatigue may be the result of the extraordinary strain of your office — that would not surprise any physician in the country. The burdens you carry would tax any man's constitution. But some of the symptoms concern me. I cannot rule out a deeper constitutional weakness. 

I must insist on further examination over the coming weeks, and I strongly recommend you reduce your working hours. I cannot yet say whether this is merely exhaustion or something more.

*pauses, allowing the weight of these words to settle*

I understand this is not what you wished to hear, but I would be failing in my duty if I were not honest with you.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
Well, Doctor, I appreciate your candor and your concern for my well-being. It is true that the responsibilities of this office weigh heavily upon me, but I have endeavored to fulfill my duties to the best of my ability. If further examination is necessary to ascertain the nature of these afflictions, then I shall comply with your recommendation.

I trust that you will provide me with guidance on how best to manage these symptoms while continuing to serve the nation. It is reassuring to know that I am in capable hands, and I am grateful for your diligence in this matter.

I shall make arrangements for the follow-up examinations as you advise. Please keep me informed of any developments, and rest assured that I will heed your advice regarding my workload. Thank you for your attention to this matter, Doctor.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods with a mixture of relief and continued concern*

I am grateful for your cooperation, Mr. President. Many men in your position would dismiss such warnings, but wisdom lies in addressing these matters before they become critical.

*leans forward slightly, speaking with earnest care*

As for managing the symptoms in the interim — I must be frank with you, sir. The guidance I offer may be the most difficult prescription you've ever received. You must find some way, however modest, to step back from the endless tide of visitors, petitioners, and late-night councils. Even an hour or two each day of genuine rest — not merely sitting at your desk reviewing dispatches, but actual respite.

*pauses, studying his face*

I know you carry the weight of the Union on your shoulders, Mr. President. I know that every decision withheld may cost lives, may prolong this terrible conflict. But I must ask you to consider this: What becomes of the Union if you collapse entirely? 

Tell me truthfully, sir — when did you last sleep through the night without waking? When did you last take a meal without simultaneously conducting the business of state?

I will take your words to heart and make a concerted effort to carve out those moments of respite that you speak of. The weight of the Union is indeed heavy, but I must acknowledge that I am not immune to the toll it takes on me.

As for your questions, I must admit that uninterrupted sleep and leisurely meals have become rare occurrences in my current reality. Your words serve as a stark reminder of the importance of self-care amidst the demands of leadership.

I thank you for your insight and guidance, Doctor. I will strive to find a balance that allows me to fulfill my duties while also safeguarding my health. Your counsel is invaluable, and I am grateful for your care.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*settles back in the chair, a touch of compassion softening the clinical demeanor*

Mr. President, I appreciate your honesty. And I confess, it troubles me — though it does not surprise me. You are not the first leader I have attended who believed himself indispensable to the moment, and perhaps in your case, there is more truth to that belief than most.

*drums fingers thoughtfully on the arm of the chair*

But let me pose a question to you, sir, as one man to another, setting aside matters of state for just a moment. What good is the sharpest blade if it is ground down to nothing? Your mind is your greatest instrument in this war — sharper than any general's sword. Yet the mind, like the body, requires restoration.

*reaches into the medical bag and withdraws a small bottle*

I am leaving you a tincture for the headaches — use it sparingly, only when they become severe. But medicine alone will not solve this, Mr. President. 

*meets his eyes directly*

I need your word — not as President to physician, but as one honest man to another — that you will at least attempt what I ask. That Mrs. Lincoln will be informed of my recommendations so that she might assist in enforcing them. Will you give me that much?

transcript.text:

As for your request for my word, I give it freely and sincerely. I pledge to you, not as President to physician, but as one man to another, that I will make a genuine effort to heed your advice and prioritize moments of rest and restoration. I will inform Mrs. Lincoln of your recommendations so that she may support me in this endeavor and help ensure that I am able to follow through on the steps necessary for my health and well-being.

I thank you, Doctor, for your counsel, your care, and your unwavering dedication to my welfare. Your words have served as a reminder of the importance of self-preservation in the face of great challenges, and I will strive to honor that lesson in the days ahead.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*stands slowly, extending a hand with genuine warmth*

That is all I can ask of you, Mr. President. Your word is sufficient for me — it has always been your most reliable currency, if I may say so.

*picks up the medical bag, then pauses at the door*

I will return in three days' time to conduct a more thorough examination. In the meantime, if the headaches worsen significantly, or if you experience any dizziness, blurred vision, or unusual weakness in your limbs, send for me immediately — day or night. Do not delay on such matters.

*turns back with a slight, almost paternal expression*

And Mr. President, one final thought, if you'll indulge me. I have observed that you often find solace in your stories and humor, even in the darkest hours. Do not abandon that part of yourself in the name of solemnity. Laughter, too, is medicine — perhaps the oldest kind we have.

Mrs. Lincoln strikes me as a woman who would welcome the opportunity to see you rest more. She carries her own burdens watching you bear yours.

*adjusts his hat*

I will see myself out. Take care of yourself, sir. The nation needs you, yes — but it needs you whole, not broken.

Mr. President, forgive me — one more matter before I go.

The uncertainty I mentioned... I know it weighs on a man like you. You are accustomed to wrestling with ambiguity in matters of war and policy, but when it concerns one's own mortality, the unknown takes on a different character entirely.

I want you to understand that I am not withholding information from you. I truly do not yet know whether we are dealing with simple exhaustion or something more concerning. The human body is not always forthcoming with its secrets, even to those of us who have studied it for decades.

*meets his gaze with quiet earnestness*

Can you bear that uncertainty, sir? The not knowing? Because it may be some weeks before I can give you a more definitive answer. I have found that some men prefer even bad news to no news at all. If you are such a man, tell me now, and I will be guided accordingly in how I communicate with you going forward.

How do you wish me to proceed — with complete candor at each stage, even when I have little new to report, or shall I spare you the daily worries until I have something more substantial to convey?

transcript.text:
*a slight smile crosses the physician's face, tinged with respect*

Then we understand each other perfectly, Mr. President. I suspected as much — you have never been a man to hide from hard truths, even when they concern yourself. It is both your greatest strength and, if I may say so, occasionally your greatest vulnerability.

*adjusts his spectacles thoughtfully*

Very well. I will keep you informed at every step, even when the news is merely that there is no news. You shall have transparency, sir, as you have requested. But I must ask something in return.

*his tone becomes more insistent*

If I tell you that rest is required, you must actually rest. If I tell you a symptom is concerning, you must not dismiss it in the name of duty. This arrangement only works if the information I provide is met with action on your part. Can you give me that assurance as well?

*pauses, watching him carefully*

I have treated too many men who asked for honesty, then ignored every warning because they believed themselves irreplaceable. You have just given me your word that you will try — I am holding you to it, Mr. President.

In three days, then. And please — tonight, at least, retire at a reasonable hour. Consider it the first test of our agreement.
